learn.hook: Tell a pilot '500 km' and she'll ask: 'Which way?' Many quantities need a direction to make sense.
points: Motion in two or three dimensions needs vectors to describe position, velocity and acceleration. This chapter builds vector tools, then applies them to constant-acceleration motion, projectiles and uniform circular motion.
Scalars have only magnitude and combine by ordinary algebra: mass, time, temperature, work, energy, speed.
Vectors have magnitude and direction and add by the triangle or parallelogram law: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum.
Notation: a vector is written in bold (A) or with an arrow (A⃗). Its magnitude is |A| or simply A, always non-negative.

example.q: A box of mass 5 kg and another of 3 kg are put together. Two forces of 5 N and 3 N act on a body. Why is the total mass surely 8 kg but the total force not surely 8 N?
steps: Mass is a scalar: masses add by ordinary algebra, 5 + 3 = 8 kg.
Force is a vector: the result depends on the angle between the forces.
It can be anything from 2 N (opposite) to 8 N (same direction).
example.answer: Mass adds simply; forces add as vectors (2 N to 8 N)

learn.reallife: Air-traffic controllers at Delhi's IGI Airport give pilots headings and speeds: velocity vectors, not just speeds.

options: Masses should be added as vectors
Displacements are vectors; the resultant is 5 m, not 7 m
quiz.explain: Masses are scalars (7 kg is right). Perpendicular displacements combine to √(3² + 4²) = 5 m.

quiz.explain: Speed is a scalar; velocity is a vector.

teach.nudge: What does a vector have that a scalar does not? And how do vectors add?

topics.title: Position and displacement vectors, equality and scaling

learn.hook: Whether you take the highway or the village road from Jaipur to Ajmer, your displacement vector is exactly the same.
points: The position vector r of a point P is the arrow from the origin O to P.
Displacement is the vector from the initial position P to the final position Q: Δr = r_Q − r_P. It depends only on the end points, not on the path.
Two vectors are equal if they have the same magnitude and the same direction. Such free vectors can be shifted parallel to themselves.
λA: if λ > 0, the magnitude becomes λ|A| and the direction is unchanged. If λ < 0, the magnitude becomes |λ||A| and the direction reverses.

example.q: A = 3 m due east. Describe 2A and −1.5A.
steps: The minus sign reverses the direction: west.

learn.reallife: Google Maps may show three routes from Bengaluru to Mysuru with different distances, but the straight-line displacement between the cities is fixed.

teach.ask: Gappu thinks his displacement from his nest to the river depends on how many trees he flies around. Explain position vector, displacement and equal vectors.
teach.praise: Displacement only cares about start and finish, and equal vectors match in size and direction. Got it!
teach.nudge: Does the path matter for displacement? And when are two vectors equal?

learn.hook: Ships at Visakhapatnam port used to plot courses with rulers and protractors: arrows placed head to tail on a chart.
points: Multiplying a vector by a scalar with dimensions gives a new physical quantity: velocity v × time t = displacement; mass × velocity = momentum.
Triangle (head-to-tail) method: place the tail of B at the head of A; the resultant R = A + B runs from the tail of A to the head of B.
Parallelogram method: draw A and B from a common point; the diagonal from that point is A + B. It gives the same result as the triangle method.
Addition is commutative (A + B = B + A) and associative ((A + B) + C = A + (B + C)).
Null vector 0 has zero magnitude: A + 0 = A, λ0 = 0, 0A = 0. Also A + (−A) = 0.

example.q: A car moves at 20 m s⁻¹ due north for 30 s. What displacement vector results?
steps: Displacement = v × t (vector × scalar with dimension of time).

learn.reallife: Rowing teams on the Hooghly feel vector addition directly: the boat's velocity relative to water adds to the river's flow.

quiz.q: Which property of the null vector is correct?

teach.ask: Gappu has two arrows, 3 cm and 4 cm long, and wants to add them. Show him the triangle and parallelogram methods.
teach.praise: Head to tail, or draw a parallelogram and take the diagonal. Same answer either way!
teach.nudge: Where do you place the second arrow? And which diagonal of the parallelogram is the sum?

topics.title: Vector subtraction and the rain–umbrella problem

learn.hook: Standing at a bus stop in a Mumbai monsoon with the wind blowing? Vector addition tells you exactly how to tilt your umbrella.
points: Subtraction is addition of the negative: A − B = A + (−B).
In the parallelogram of A and B, the second diagonal gives A − B (from the head of B to the head of A).
|A − B| = √(A² + B² − 2AB cos θ), where θ is the angle between A and B.

Rain falling vertically at v_r and wind blowing horizontally at v_w give the rain a resultant velocity at angle θ to the vertical with tan θ = v_w/v_r. Tilt the umbrella towards where the rain comes from, at angle θ from the vertical.

example.q: Rain falls vertically at 8 m s⁻¹. Wind starts blowing from west to east at 6 m s⁻¹. How should you hold your umbrella?
steps: The rain now has components 8 m s⁻¹ down and 6 m s⁻¹ eastward.
tan θ = 6/8 = 0.75, θ ≈ 37° from the vertical.
The rain comes from the west, so tilt the umbrella towards the west at about 37° from the vertical.
example.answer: Tilted ~37° from the vertical towards the west

learn.reallife: During the Kerala monsoon, slanting rain against shopfronts is just the resultant of the falling speed and the wind velocity.

topics.title: Resolution of vectors and unit vectors

learn.hook: A rope pulling a cart at an angle does two jobs at once: it drags it forward and lifts it slightly. Resolving the force reveals both.
points: Any vector in a plane can be written as a sum of two vectors along any two non-collinear directions: A = λa + μb.
Unit vectors î, ĵ, k̂ point along x, y, z, have magnitude 1 and no dimensions or units; they only show direction.
Rectangular components: Aₓ = A cos θ, A_y = A sin θ, where θ is the angle with the +x axis. A = Aₓî + A_yĵ.
Back from components: A = √(Aₓ² + A_y²), tan θ = A_y/Aₓ.
In 3D: A = Aₓî + A_yĵ + A_zk̂, A = √(Aₓ² + A_y² + A_z²); direction cosines cos α = Aₓ/A, cos β = A_y/A, cos γ = A_z/A, with cos²α + cos²β + cos²γ = 1.

example.q: A force of 10 N acts at 30° above the +x axis. Find its components.

learn.reallife: Civil engineers designing the cable-stayed Signature Bridge in Delhi resolve each cable's tension into vertical (holding the deck) and horizontal parts.

quiz.explain: Unit vectors only give direction; they are pure numbers of size 1.

Assertion (A): A vector can be resolved along any two non-collinear directions in its plane.
Reason (R): Any two non-collinear vectors can be scaled and added to give any vector in that plane.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false

quiz.explain: Using the parallelogram law with two non-parallel directions, any planar vector can be built. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks resolution is possible only along perpendicular axes

teach.ask: Gappu wants to break a slanted force into 'how much forward' and 'how much up'. Teach him resolution and unit vectors.
teach.praise: Cos for the side next to the angle, sin for the opposite side, and î, ĵ just point the way!
teach.nudge: Which trig function gives the x-component? How do you get the magnitude back from the components?

learn.hook: A motorboat aiming straight across the Brahmaputra lands far downstream. The analytical method tells you exactly where.
points: Component method: if A = Aₓî + A_yĵ and B = Bₓî + B_yĵ, then R = (Aₓ + Bₓ)î + (A_y + B_y)ĵ.
Law of cosines: R² = A² + B² + 2AB cos θ, where θ is the angle between A and B.
Law of sines: R/sin θ = A/sin β = B/sin α, where α is the angle between R and A. Also tan α = B sin θ/(A + B cos θ).
Special cases: θ = 0 → R = A + B; θ = 180° → R = |A − B|; θ = 90° → R = √(A² + B²).

example.q: A boat moves at 8 km h⁻¹ due north in still water. The river flows east at 6 km h⁻¹. Find the boat's resultant velocity.
steps: tan α = 6/8 = 0.75, α ≈ 37° east of north.
example.answer: 10 km h⁻¹ at about 37° east of north

learn.reallife: Ferries crossing from Mumbai's Gateway of India to Elephanta adjust their heading for the tidal current using this exact calculation.

topics.title: Position and velocity in a plane

learn.hook: A drone delivering medicines in Telangana's 'Medicine from the Sky' project needs its x and y coordinates and velocity components every second.
points: Position vector r = xî + yĵ; displacement Δr = Δxî + Δyĵ.
Average velocity v̄ = Δr/Δt. Instantaneous velocity v = dr/dt = vₓî + v_yĵ, with vₓ = dx/dt and v_y = dy/dt.
Instantaneous velocity is always along the tangent to the path, in the direction of motion.
Speed |v| = √(vₓ² + v_y²) and direction tan θ = v_y/vₓ (θ measured from the x-axis).

example.q: r = 3t î + 2t² ĵ (SI units). Find the velocity and speed at t = 1 s.
steps: At t = 1 s: v = 3 î + 4 ĵ m s⁻¹.
Speed = √(9 + 16) = 5 m s⁻¹, at tan⁻¹(4/3) ≈ 53° to the x-axis.

learn.reallife: A Formula Bharat student race car's GPS logs x and y every 0.1 s; dividing each Δr by Δt gives the velocity arrows shown on the team's laptop.

Reason (R): Instantaneous velocity is always along the tangent to the path of motion.

teach.ask: Gappu knows his x and y at every second as he flies. Teach him how to get his velocity vector and speed.
teach.praise: Differentiate x and y, then use Pythagoras for speed. And my velocity always hugs the tangent!
teach.nudge: How do you get vₓ and v_y from x and y? Which way does the velocity point?

learn.hook: At the top of a cricket ball's flight, velocity is horizontal but acceleration is straight down: they can be at any angle.
points: Average acceleration ā = Δv/Δt. Instantaneous acceleration a = dv/dt = aₓî + a_yĵ, with aₓ = dvₓ/dt, a_y = dv_y/dt.
In two dimensions v and a can make any angle: 0° (speeding up straight), 180° (slowing straight), 90° (uniform circular motion), or anything else (projectile).
Recipe: from r(t), differentiate once for v(t), again for a(t); then find magnitudes with Pythagoras and directions with tan θ.
Acceleration is not necessarily along velocity; it points the way velocity is changing.

example.q: r = 2t î + t³ ĵ (SI units). Find a at t = 1 s.
steps: At t = 1 s, a = 6 ĵ m s⁻², i.e. 6 m s⁻² along +y.

learn.reallife: A Chandrayaan orbiter's velocity is along its orbit while its acceleration points towards the Moon's centre: perpendicular, not parallel.

For a body in uniform circular motion, the angle between v and a is
quiz.explain: v is tangential and a points to the centre, so they are perpendicular.
quiz.mistake: Thinks acceleration is along the velocity

quiz.q: In two-dimensional motion, the angle between velocity and acceleration
quiz.explain: Acceleration points the way the velocity changes, which can be at any angle.
quiz.mistake: Carries over the 1D idea that a is along v

quiz.q: r = t² î + t² ĵ (SI units). The direction of acceleration makes what angle with the x-axis?
quiz.explain: a = 2î + 2ĵ; equal components give 45°.

quiz.q: For r = (t³) î + (2t²) ĵ (SI units), aₓ at t = 1 s in m s⁻² is
quiz.explain: vₓ = 3t², aₓ = 6t = 6 m s⁻².

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A body can have acceleration perpendicular to its velocity.
Reason (R): In uniform circular motion, acceleration is towards the centre while velocity is tangential.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Uniform circular motion is the standard example, so R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks acceleration must be along velocity

teach.ask: Gappu thinks acceleration always points where he is flying. Explain acceleration in a plane with an example where it doesn't.
teach.praise: So my acceleration points where my velocity is changing, which can be sideways! Like circling a tree.
teach.nudge: How is acceleration defined in 2D? Does it always point along the velocity?

topics.title: Motion in a plane with constant acceleration

learn.hook: A puck pushed across ice while a steady wind blows sideways: two simple 1D problems hiding inside one 2D problem.
points: With constant acceleration a: v = v₀ + at and r = r₀ + v₀t + ½at² (vector forms).
Component form: x = x₀ + v₀ₓt + ½aₓt² and y = y₀ + v₀ᵧt + ½a_yt². The x and y motions are independent; time t links them.
To find something at a given x-coordinate, first solve the x-equation for t, then use that t in the y-equations.
Speed = √(vₓ² + v_y²) at the required time.

example.q: A particle starts from the origin with v₀ = 4 î m s⁻¹ and constant a = 2 ĵ m s⁻². Find its position and speed at t = 3 s.

learn.reallife: Satellite launch trajectories from Sriharikota are split into downrange and altitude components, each solved with 1D kinematics in short steps.

games.title: Find y when the particle reaches a given x
items: Write x(t) = x₀ + v₀ₓt + ½aₓt²
Put in the given x and solve for t
Write y(t) = y₀ + v₀ᵧt + ½a_yt²
Substitute that t to get y
Use vₓ and v_y at that t for speed if needed

games.title: Independent motions
items: In 2D constant-acceleration motion, x and y motions affect each other's acceleration.
They are independent.
The same time t appears in both x and y equations.
Time links the components.
r = r₀ + v₀t + ½at² is valid only for constant a.
Like its 1D version.
If aₓ = 0, the x-velocity stays constant.
No acceleration along x.
Speed in 2D equals vₓ + v_y.
Use √(vₓ² + v_y²).

quiz.q: A particle starts from rest at the origin with a = 3î + 4ĵ m s⁻². Its distance from the origin after 2 s, in m, is
quiz.mistake: Forgets the ½ or the t²

quiz.q: A particle has v₀ = 5 î m s⁻¹ and a = 2 ĵ m s⁻² (constant), starting at the origin. Its y-coordinate when x = 10 m, in m, is
For the same particle (v₀ = 5î m s⁻¹, a = 2ĵ m s⁻²), its speed at t = 2 s in m s⁻¹ is (√41 ≈ 6.40)
A particle has v₀ = 10ĵ m s⁻¹ and a = 2î m s⁻². Its velocity at t = 5 s is
quiz.explain: v = v₀ + at = 10ĵ + 10î.

quiz.q: Why can 2D constant-acceleration motion be treated as two 1D motions?
options: The x and y components of the vector equations are independent
Because the path is always straight
Because x and y are always equal
quiz.explain: Each component equation contains only its own components, linked only by t.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the path must be straight

quiz.q: A particle starts at r₀ = 2î m with v₀ = 3ĵ m s⁻¹ and a = 0. Its position at t = 4 s is
quiz.explain: r = r₀ + v₀t = 2î + 12ĵ m.

quiz.q: A particle starts from rest at the origin with a = 6î + 8ĵ m s⁻². Its speed after 3 s in m s⁻¹ is
quiz.explain: |a| = 10 m s⁻², v = at = 30 m s⁻¹ (from rest, along a).

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A body with v₀ = 4î m s⁻¹ and constant a = 2ĵ m s⁻² keeps vₓ = 4 m s⁻¹ throughout.
Reason (R): The magnitude of its acceleration is 2 m s⁻².
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, but the size of the acceleration is not the reason; vₓ stays fixed because the acceleration has no x-component.
quiz.mistake: Uses a true but irrelevant fact as the reason

teach.ask: Gappu is pushed east and a steady breeze accelerates him north. He can't work out where he'll be. Show him the component method.
teach.praise: Split into x and y, solve each, and use the same time. 2D problems are just two 1D problems!
teach.nudge: Can you treat x and y separately? What connects them?

topics.title: Projectile motion: independence and the parabolic path

learn.hook: Hit a ball and drop another at the same instant from the same height: both land together. Horizontal speed doesn't change falling time.
points: A projectile moves under gravity alone after launch (air resistance ignored).
Horizontal motion is uniform (aₓ = 0); vertical motion is uniformly accelerated (a_y = −g). They are independent.
Launched with speed v₀ at angle θ₀: vₓ = v₀ cos θ₀ (constant), v_y = v₀ sin θ₀ − gt; x = (v₀ cos θ₀)t, y = (v₀ sin θ₀)t − ½gt².
Eliminating t: y = x tan θ₀ − gx²/(2v₀² cos²θ₀). This is of the form y = ax − bx², a parabola.

example.q: A ball is projected at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30° (g = 10 m s⁻²). Find vₓ, v_y and the position at t = 1 s.

learn.reallife: Javelin star Neeraj Chopra's throw follows a near-parabolic path; air drag and lift make the real path a bit shorter and lopsided.

games.title: Constant or changing during projectile flight?
items: Horizontal velocity
Acceleration
Vertical velocity
Speed
Height
Direction of velocity

games.title: Projectile basics
items: A projectile's acceleration is g downward throughout the flight.
Only gravity acts.
The horizontal velocity decreases as the projectile rises.
With no air resistance, vₓ is constant.
The path of a projectile is a parabola.
y = ax − bx².
At the highest point, the speed of a projectile is zero.
vₓ = v₀ cos θ₀ remains.
A ball dropped and a ball thrown horizontally from the same height land at the same time.
Vertical motions are identical.

quiz.q: At the highest point of a projectile's path, the velocity is
options: Horizontal, equal to v₀ cos θ₀
quiz.explain: v_y = 0 at the top, but vₓ = v₀ cos θ₀ remains.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the projectile stops at the top

quiz.q: A projectile is launched at 40 m s⁻¹ at 60° (cos 60° = 0.5). Its horizontal velocity after 2 s, in m s⁻¹, is
quiz.explain: vₓ = v₀ cos θ₀ = 20 m s⁻¹ and never changes.

quiz.q: The acceleration of a projectile at the top of its path is
quiz.explain: Gravity acts all the time, so a = g downward everywhere.

quiz.q: The trajectory y = x tan θ₀ − gx²/(2v₀² cos²θ₀) shows that the path is a
quiz.explain: y = ax − bx² is the equation of a parabola.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the path with a circular arc

quiz.q: A ball is thrown at 20 m s⁻¹ at 30° (g = 10 m s⁻²). Its vertical velocity after 0.5 s in m s⁻¹ is
quiz.explain: v_y = v₀ sin θ₀ − gt = 10 − 5 = 5 m s⁻¹.

quiz.q: For the same ball (20 m s⁻¹ at 30°, g = 10 m s⁻²), the height after 1 s in m is
quiz.explain: y = (v₀ sin θ₀)t − ½gt² = 10 − 5 = 5 m.

quiz.q: Which assumption is made in simple projectile motion?
options: Air resistance is negligible and g is constant
quiz.explain: Ignoring air drag and taking g constant gives the clean parabolic equations.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile are independent.
Reason (R): Gravity acts only vertically, so it changes v_y but not vₓ.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Since the only force is vertical, the horizontal motion is unaffected. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks gravity slows the forward motion

teach.ask: Gappu throws a berry forward and thinks gravity slows it horizontally too. Explain independence of motions and why the path is a parabola.
teach.praise: Horizontal stays steady, vertical feels gravity, and together they draw a parabola. Berry physics!
teach.nudge: What happens to horizontal velocity during flight? And what shape does the path make?

topics.title: Time of flight, maximum height and range

learn.hook: Why does a fielder's throw angle matter so much? Because range depends on sin 2θ, and for a launch from ground level without air resistance, 45° gives the maximum range.
points: Time to reach maximum height t_m = v₀ sin θ₀/g; total time of flight T_f = 2v₀ sin θ₀/g.
Maximum height h_m = v₀² sin²θ₀/(2g).
Horizontal range R = v₀² sin 2θ₀/g. It is maximum at θ₀ = 45°: R_max = v₀²/g.
Complementary angles θ and (90° − θ) give the same range (sin 2θ = sin(180° − 2θ)), but different heights and flight times.
Real throws (cricket ball, javelin) face air resistance, which reduces range and height; the best angle is then a little less than 45°.

example.q: A cricketer can throw a ball to a maximum horizontal distance of 100 m. How high can he throw it vertically with the same speed? (g = 10 m s⁻²)
steps: R_max = v₀²/g = 100 m → v₀² = 1000 m² s⁻².

learn.reallife: A fielder's throw from the boundary at the Eden Gardens is slightly flatter than 45° because air drag steals more range from higher throws.

items.q: v₀ = 20 m/s at 30°: time of flight (s)

quiz.q: A ball is projected at 30 m s⁻¹ at 45° (g = 10 m s⁻²). Its range in m is
A projectile is launched at 50 m s⁻¹ at 30° (g = 10 m s⁻²). The time of flight in s is
quiz.mistake: Gives the time to reach the top

quiz.q: For the same projectile (50 m s⁻¹ at 30°, g = 10 m s⁻²), the maximum height in m is
quiz.mistake: Forgets to square sin θ₀ or the 2 in 2g

quiz.q: Two projectiles are launched with the same speed at 25° and 65°. Their ranges are
quiz.explain: 25° and 65° are complementary, so sin 2θ is the same (sin 50° = sin 130°).
quiz.mistake: Thinks the higher angle always goes farther

quiz.q: At what angle of projection are the horizontal range and the maximum height equal?
quiz.explain: v₀² sin 2θ/g = v₀² sin²θ/(2g) → 2 sin θ cos θ = sin²θ/2 → tan θ = 4.

quiz.q: The maximum range of a gun is 2 km. The shell's launch speed in m s⁻¹ (g = 10 m s⁻²) is about
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert km to m or the square root

quiz.q: When air resistance is included, the range of a long throw
options: Decreases, and the best angle is a little less than 45°
quiz.explain: Drag removes energy and momentum, cutting range; the optimum angle drops below 45°.
quiz.mistake: Ignores air resistance in real sports

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): For a given launch speed, the horizontal range is maximum at 45°.
Reason (R): At 45° the time of flight is maximum.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true (sin 2θ₀ = 1). R is false: the time of flight 2v₀ sin θ₀/g is greatest at 90°.
quiz.mistake: Thinks maximum range means maximum flight time

teach.ask: Gappu wants to fling a seed as far as possible. Teach him time of flight, maximum height and range, and the best angle.
teach.praise: 45° gives the longest flight, and 30° and 60° tie on range. My seeds will travel far!
teach.nudge: Which angle gives the greatest range? Which pairs of angles give equal ranges?

learn.hook: A relief helicopter over flooded Assam must release a food packet BEFORE it is directly above the target. Here's why.
points: Thrown horizontally from height h with speed u: x = ut, y = ½gt² (measuring downward).
Time to land t = √(2h/g); horizontal distance = u√(2h/g); speed on landing = √(u² + (gt)²).
A packet dropped from a moving aircraft keeps the aircraft's horizontal velocity, so (without air drag) it stays vertically below the aircraft while falling.
To hit a target at the same level, a bullet must be aimed slightly above it, because it falls ½gt² during flight time t. A gun can reach a target only if its distance ≤ R_max = v₀²/g.

example.q: A stone is thrown horizontally at 10 m s⁻¹ from a 45 m high cliff (g = 10 m s⁻²). Find the time of flight and where it lands.
steps: x = ut = 10 × 3 = 30 m from the foot of the cliff.
At impact v_y = gt = 30 m s⁻¹, speed = √(100 + 900) ≈ 31.6 m s⁻¹.

learn.reallife: Indian Air Force supply drops in Ladakh use this physics (plus parachutes and wind corrections) to land loads on target.

games.title: Solving a horizontal-throw problem
items: Use vertical motion: h = ½gt²
Solve t = √(2h/g)
Horizontal distance x = ut
Vertical speed at landing v_y = gt
Landing speed = √(u² + v_y²)

games.title: Target facts
items: A bomb released from a plane flying horizontally lands directly below the release point.
It moves forward with the plane's horizontal speed.
Horizontal launch speed does not affect the time to fall from a given height.
Time depends only on h and g.
A bullet fired horizontally at a target 100 m away hits slightly below the aim point.
It falls under gravity during the flight.
A gun whose maximum range is 3 km can hit a target 5 km away by changing the angle.
No angle gives more than R_max.
Without air drag, a dropped packet stays vertically below the plane.
Same horizontal velocity.

quiz.q: A ball rolls off a 20 m high table-top cliff at 5 m s⁻¹ (g = 10 m s⁻²). The time to reach the ground in s is
quiz.explain: t = √(2h/g) = √(40/10) = 2 s; the horizontal speed does not matter.

quiz.q: A ball rolls off the edge of a 20 m high cliff at 5 m s⁻¹ (g = 10 m s⁻²). The horizontal distance it covers before landing in m is
A plane flying horizontally at 100 m s⁻¹ at a height of 500 m drops a packet (g = 10 m s⁻²). How far ahead of the target (horizontally) should it be released, in m?
quiz.explain: t = √(2 × 500/10) = 10 s; horizontal distance = 100 × 10 = 1000 m.

quiz.q: A bullet is fired horizontally at 200 m s⁻¹ at a target 100 m away at the same height (g = 9.8 m s⁻²). By how much (in m) does it fall below the aim point?
A bullet fired at 30° lands 3 km away. The maximum range with the same speed (sin 60° = 0.866) is about (in km)
quiz.explain: R = R_max sin 60° → R_max = 3/0.866 ≈ 3.46 km.

quiz.q: A gun's shell fired at 30° lands 3 km away. Can the same gun, with the same muzzle speed, hit a target 5 km away by changing only the angle?
options: No, because 5 km exceeds the maximum range of about 3.46 km
quiz.explain: No angle gives more than R_max ≈ 3.46 km.
quiz.mistake: Thinks changing the angle can always increase range

quiz.q: A stone thrown horizontally at 15 m s⁻¹ hits the ground after 2 s (g = 10 m s⁻²). Its landing speed in m s⁻¹ is
quiz.explain: v_y = gt = 20 m s⁻¹; speed = √(15² + 20²) = 25 m s⁻¹.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Two stones thrown horizontally with different speeds from the same height land at the same time.
Reason (R): The time of fall depends only on the height and g, not on the horizontal velocity.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: t = √(2h/g) for both. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the faster stone takes longer

teach.ask: Gappu wants to drop a berry on his friend below while flying forward. He plans to drop it when he is right above. Explain why that fails.
teach.praise: The berry keeps my forward speed, so I must let go early. My friend is in for a treat!
teach.nudge: Does the berry keep moving forward after release? How do you find how long it falls?

topics.title: Uniform circular motion: angular speed, period and frequency

learn.hook: A ceiling fan, a Ferris wheel at a Dussehra mela and the Earth's spin all share one set of simple formulas.
points: Uniform circular motion (UCM): constant speed on a circle. Speed is constant but velocity keeps changing direction.
Angular displacement Δθ (in radians); angular speed ω = dθ/dt (rad s⁻¹). Linear speed v = Rω.
Period T is the time for one revolution; frequency ν = 1/T (Hz or rev s⁻¹). ω = 2π/T = 2πν, v = 2πRν.
Centripetal acceleration a_c = v²/R = ω²R = 4π²ν²R.

example.q: A stone tied to a 0.5 m string is whirled at ω = 4 rad s⁻¹. Find its speed and centripetal acceleration.

learn.reallife: A washing machine's drum spinning at 1200 rpm (20 rev s⁻¹) has ω = 40π rad s⁻¹, enough to fling water out of clothes.

quiz.q: A particle moves on a circle of radius 3 m with angular speed 2 rad s⁻¹. Its linear speed in m s⁻¹ is
quiz.explain: v = Rω = 3 × 2 = 6 m s⁻¹.

quiz.q: A wheel makes 10 revolutions in 5 s. Its frequency in Hz is
quiz.explain: ν = revolutions/time = 10/5 = 2 Hz.

quiz.q: A body moves on a circle of radius 2 m at 4 m s⁻¹. Its centripetal acceleration in m s⁻² is
quiz.explain: a_c = v²/R = 16/2 = 8 m s⁻².

quiz.q: A stone in a circular groove of radius 0.25 m completes one round every 2 s. Its angular speed in units of π rad s⁻¹ is
quiz.explain: ω = 2π/T = 2π/2 = π rad s⁻¹.

quiz.q: For a particle in uniform circular motion, which quantity is constant?
quiz.explain: Only the magnitude of velocity (speed) is constant; directions keep changing.
quiz.mistake: Thinks velocity is constant when speed is

quiz.q: ω = 10 rad s⁻¹ and R = 0.2 m. The centripetal acceleration in m s⁻² is
The period of a body in UCM is 0.2 s. Its frequency in Hz is

Assertion (A): In uniform circular motion, the velocity of the body changes continuously.
Reason (R): The direction of motion changes at every point even though the speed is constant.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Velocity is a vector; its direction changes along the circle. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks constant speed means constant velocity

teach.ask: Gappu spins on a merry-go-round and is puzzled: 'My speed is constant, so where is the acceleration?' Explain angular speed, period, frequency and v = Rω.
teach.praise: Speed steady, direction changing, so velocity changes. And ω = 2π/T links it all!
teach.nudge: If speed is constant, what about velocity changes? How are ω, T and ν connected?

learn.hook: A centrifuge at an AIIMS blood bank can produce accelerations over 1000 times g, all pointing towards the centre.
points: Derivation: in time Δt the velocity turns through Δθ; the triangle of velocity vectors is similar to the triangle of position vectors, so |Δv|/v = |Δr|/R.
Dividing by Δt and letting Δt → 0: a = v·(v/R) = v²/R, directed towards the centre (Δv points inward in the limit).
Magnitude v²/R is constant, but the direction keeps changing (always towards the centre), so the centripetal acceleration is NOT a constant vector.
Only in uniform circular motion is the net acceleration purely radial; if speed changes, there is also a tangential component.

example.q: A centrifuge spins a tube at radius 0.1 m with ω = 100 rad s⁻¹. Find the centripetal acceleration in units of g (g = 10 m s⁻²).

learn.reallife: The Moon's centripetal acceleration towards the Earth is only about 0.0027 m s⁻², yet it keeps the Moon in orbit around us.

games.title: Derivation of a = v²/R
items: Draw positions r and r′ and velocities v and v′ separated by angle Δθ
Note the velocity triangle is similar to the position triangle
Write |Δv|/v = |Δr|/R
Divide by Δt and take the limit Δt → 0
Get a = v²/R towards the centre

games.title: Circular-motion statements
items: In uniform circular motion, the acceleration is constant in magnitude.
a = v²/R stays the same.
The centripetal acceleration vector is constant in uniform circular motion.
Its direction changes continuously.
The net acceleration of a particle in any circular motion is always towards the centre.
Only for uniform circular motion.
The velocity and acceleration are perpendicular in uniform circular motion.
Tangent vs radius.
A body on a circle with increasing speed has a tangential acceleration component.
Speed is changing.

quiz.q: The centripetal acceleration of a body in uniform circular motion is directed
options: Towards the centre of the circle
quiz.explain: Δv points inward in the limit, so a is towards the centre.

quiz.q: If the speed of a body in UCM is doubled (same radius), its centripetal acceleration becomes how many times the original?
quiz.explain: a = v²/R, so doubling v gives 4 times a.

quiz.q: Which statement about centripetal acceleration in UCM is correct?
options: Its magnitude is constant but its direction changes
It is zero because speed is constant
quiz.explain: Magnitude v²/R is fixed, but it always points to the centre, a changing direction.
quiz.mistake: Treats constant magnitude as a constant vector

quiz.q: A car goes round a circular track of radius 100 m at 20 m s⁻¹. Its centripetal acceleration in m s⁻² is
A particle moves on a circle with increasing speed. Its acceleration is
options: Neither purely radial nor purely tangential
quiz.explain: It has a centripetal (radial) part v²/R and a tangential part dv/dt.
quiz.mistake: Applies the UCM result to non-uniform motion

quiz.q: In the derivation of a = v²/R, the key step uses
options: Similar triangles formed by position and velocity vectors
quiz.explain: The angle between r and r′ equals that between v and v′, so the triangles are similar.

quiz.q: A centrifuge has R = 0.05 m and ω = 200 rad s⁻¹. The centripetal acceleration in m s⁻² is

Assertion (A): The centripetal acceleration in uniform circular motion is not a constant vector.
Reason (R): Its magnitude v²/R keeps changing during the motion.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true because its direction changes. R is false: in uniform circular motion the magnitude v²/R is constant.

teach.ask: Gappu circles a tree at constant speed and insists his acceleration is a constant vector because its size doesn't change. Correct him and show where a = v²/R comes from.
teach.praise: So my acceleration's size is fixed, but it keeps swivelling to face the tree. Not a constant vector!
teach.nudge: Where does the acceleration point? Its size is fixed, but what about its direction?
